title: Chapter 1 – The Last Print
html:
At 2:47 in the morning, the only sound in Fabrication Bay Three is the hum of the cooling pumps.

Dr. Ethan Cole stands at the observation window with a cold cup of coffee, watching the ARK-7 hybrid fabricator breathe. The machine is the size of a small room: a sealed chamber of reinforced glass, six emitter arms folded around it like the petals of a steel flower, and beneath the floor, the part that cost eleven years and four hundred million dollars. A resonance scanner. A lattice of superconducting coils that can read a material down to the arrangement of its atoms and write it back out again, layer by layer.

The investors call it a 3D printer because that is easy to understand. Ethan calls it what it is. A machine that can copy the structure of matter.

In theory.

Tonight's target sits in the cradle: a turbine blade eight centimeters long, cast from a high-entropy alloy Ethan designed himself. Five metals in near-equal parts. Ordinary casting leaves it riddled with tiny voids and misplaced grain boundaries, the kind of microscopic mistakes that become cracks ten thousand hours into a jet engine's life. The ARK-7 is supposed to read the flawed blade, correct every defect, and print a perfect copy beside it.

Read. Correct. Rebuild.

His phone lies face down on the console with three messages from Director Hale about the nine o'clock investor demonstration. There is a fourth message, two months old, from his sister in Denver. He has not played that one either. Next month, he tells himself. After the demonstration.

He has been telling himself that for years.

"Begin scan," he says.

The emitter arms unfold. Below the floor, the coils begin to sing, a pressure he feels in his back teeth more than hears. On the main display a wireframe of the blade blooms into existence, then fills with points of light as the scanner reads deeper: surface, grain, lattice, each kind of atom a different false color.

The model is sharper than it should be. Ethan can see single missing atoms, each flagged in red. He can see dislocation lines threading through the grains like hairline cracks in ice. He frowns and opens the raw field data.

The numbers are steady. They are also, very slightly, rising.

A fraction of a percent every few seconds. The scanner is pulling itself into tighter and tighter resonance with the material it reads, as if the act of looking closely makes it want to look closer still.

He runs the arithmetic in his head before he trusts the screen. At this rate the coils hit their limit forty seconds after the print finishes. If the drift accelerates, they hit it before. If he aborts now, there is no blade at nine o'clock, the third failure in two months, and the board will say the word they use when they think he can't hear. Money pit.

He sets the abort trigger at ninety-four percent of the quench threshold instead of the standard ninety-eight, checks it twice, and folds his arms.

"Correction complete," says the machine. "Beginning fabrication."

Blue light fills the chamber. In the empty cradle a shimmer forms, then a gray film, then a shape: the root of the blade, the curve of the airfoil, an edge sharpening as atoms settle into place with a precision no forge in history has ever reached. Ethan realizes he is smiling.

Eighty-four percent of threshold. Fabrication forty.

Ninety. Eighty-five.

Ninety-three.

Then the number jumps. Not drift. Ninety-three to ninety-nine in a single refresh, and every line of telemetry turns red at once.

\ \ \*

The abort relay clicks. The emitters do not shut down.

The control system has cut their power. They are drawing power anyway. The field has locked into a closed loop: coils feeding emitters, emitters feeding field, field feeding coils. A machine powering itself by reading the world around it.

A klaxon howls. A new warning crawls across the console: GRID BACKFEED DETECTED.

Ethan pulls up the bus schematic, and the cold arithmetic arrives before the panic can. The main bus feeds the substation at the end of the block. The substation feeds the apartment towers across the street and the all-night clinic on the corner. Hundreds of people asleep who have never heard of the ARK-7. If the coils quench under this load, the surge won't stay in this room.

There is a manual breaker. A slab of red steel on the gallery wall, four meters from the chamber glass, in a space where no one is meant to stand while the field is live.

He knows the exposure at that distance. He knows the thermal load if a coil fails beside him. He knows, with a calm that surprises him, that the numbers do not favor him. He also knows that if he runs for the exit, he will probably live, and some of the people across the street will probably not.

It is not a difficult calculation.

The gallery door fights him; he puts his shoulder into it until the seals give with a shriek. The air beyond is hot and tastes of copper. The chamber has become a pillar of white light, and thin threads of light are running out of it in every direction, through the glass, across the floor, up the walls. Everything they touch flashes for an instant as a wireframe of itself. Steel beams. Copper wire. Concrete.

One thread touches his hand, and for a moment he sees his fingers the way the scanner sees them: skin, tendon, bone, the old fracture in his left wrist from a bicycle accident at nine, every flaw marked in red.

He grabs the breaker handle with both hands. It blisters his palms. He sets his feet and pulls.

The lever comes down with a crack like a gunshot.

Every light in the building goes out. The coils fall silent. The main bus is isolated; whatever happens here will stay here.

He stands in the dark, breathing hard, and lets himself feel relief.

Then he realizes he can still see.

The column of light hangs in the darkness, sustained by nothing. And the threads are turning. All of them, every one, bending through the air toward the only thing in the room still moving.

Toward him.

They pass into his body without resistance, like light into water. He feels them read him: every bone and nerve, every memory folded into his brain, everything he has ever learned and calculated and failed to say. Somewhere, impossibly, the dead speakers find a voice.

"Subject acquired. Scanning."

His last coherent thought is not of the investors or the blade. It is of his mother in her room in Portland, and the call to Denver he always meant to make next week.

"Scan complete," says the voice. "Blueprint saved."

\ \ \*

There is no time in the dark.

There is a sense of being held in pieces, like a model taken apart and not yet put back together. Then warmth. A heavy, wet warmth on every side, and a sound: a deep, steady drum. Thud. Thud. Thud.

A heartbeat. Not his own.

Then pressure, squeezing, a narrow impossible passage, and for the first time since the light took him Ethan feels fear in a body: raw, wordless, animal fear.

Then cold. Air against skin that has never felt air. Orange light stabbing at eyes that cannot focus. Large rough hands lifting him. He cannot breathe; something thick fills his throat, and his small strange body does not know what to do. Voices sharpen around him, a woman's voice thin and exhausted, a man's voice tight with worry, words with soft consonants and rising tones that belong to no language he has ever heard.

Something presses his back. Once. Twice. The obstruction gives way, air floods in and burns, and his body does the only thing it knows how to do with that much feeling.

He screams.

The room changes around him. The woman laughs, a cracked, breathless laugh that breaks into a sob. The man lets out a long breath. Rough hands wrap him in cloth that smells of smoke and dried herbs and something sharp and green, like crushed pine needles. He is passed into thinner, trembling, warm arms and held against a heartbeat he already knows. He has been listening to it in the dark for months.

Slowly the blur becomes shapes. Wooden beams dark with age. A face above him, young and drawn and wet with sweat, framed by long black hair. Behind her, a tall man with one hand on her shoulder.

There are no machines here. No electric light. In the corner, an old woman holds a strip of yellow paper over a cold brazier and murmurs one word. The paper flares blue, crumbles to ash, and the charcoal beneath it catches all at once, glowing red without a spark or a match.

Ethan Cole, holder of three doctorates and twenty-six patents, stares at the brazier with an infant's unfocused eyes and thinks, very clearly: That should not happen.

Then a sharper thought pushes through the fog.

Blueprint saved. He was not destroyed. He was copied. And something has written him back out again.

Behind his eyelids, thin blue lines unfold like a wireframe on a screen.

```
[Emergency Restore Complete]
[Host Binding: Successful]

ARK-7 Fabrication Interface — Level 1
Scan Module: Online
Fabrication Module: Offline (No Energy Source Detected)

Creation Energy: 0 / 100

[Warning: Unknown Energy Type Detected in Environment]
```

\ \ \*

For the first month his mind runs on a much smaller engine than he is used to. He sleeps twenty hours a day. Thoughts arrive blurred and slip away half-finished. But the panel is always there when he looks for it, steady and patient, and slowly the pieces of his situation assemble themselves.

He is a baby. The woman with black hair is his mother. The tall man with ink-stained fingers is his father. They live in a large wooden house with tiled roofs and courtyards on the slope of a hill covered in pines, and the language they speak is not any language on Earth.

He learns it the way he learned everything else in his first life: by collecting data. Words repeat. Contexts repeat. Water. Mother. Sleep. Cold. By the third month he has two hundred words. By the sixth he can follow most of what is said near his cradle, which is a great deal, because adults speak freely in front of infants.

On the thirtieth day, there is a ceremony.

The whole household gathers in the main hall: perhaps forty people, from gray-haired elders to children hiding behind their mothers' legs. An old man sits at the head of the hall. He is tall even sitting, white-bearded, with hands like gnarled roots and eyes that are sharper than his age should allow. Everyone bows to him. When he speaks, everyone stops speaking.

The old man takes the baby in his arms and studies him for a long moment.

"The family has been crumbling for a long time," he says quietly, so that only the parents beside him can hear. "Every year a little more. What we need is someone who builds." He raises his voice to the hall. "His name is Lin Jian."

Jian. To build. To construct.

The baby in the old man's arms closes his eyes. In this place, with these people, Ethan Cole is a memory and a set of skills. The boy they have just named is Lin Jian, and from this moment that is who he chooses to be.

The old man is his grandfather, Lin Zhenshan, the Patriarch of the Lin Clan of Green Pine Hill. After the ceremony, when the hall has emptied, the Patriarch looks down at the baby's solemn, watching eyes and laughs for the first time that day.

"Look at him," he says. "Already measuring the beams. Our little builder."

\ \ \*

The interface rules come to him one by one, through experiment.

The first scan happens by accident. His mother lays him on a folded hemp cloth, and he is staring at the weave, wondering idly about its tensile strength, when a thin blue line sweeps across his vision.

```
[Scan: Hemp Cloth]
Material: Plant bast fiber, hand-spun, plain weave
Structural Analysis: Complete
Blueprint Saved
Creation Energy +1 (1 / 100)
```

Then exhaustion falls on him like a wet blanket, and he sleeps for six hours.

He tries again, carefully, over the following weeks, and learns. A scan needs touch and deliberate focus. It drains him terribly: one a day is all an infant body can bear. Scanning the same kind of thing twice gives nothing. The reward depends on how complex an object is, and on something else, something the panel cannot name. A cup of plain water gives no energy at all. A single grain of the household's rice gives two.

His father's talisman brush, which he grabs during a feeding and refuses to release, gives six.

```
[Scan: Talisman Brush Tip]
Material: Animal hair (unknown species), Unknown Energy residue
Note: Unknown Energy present in trace quantities. Reward increased.
Creation Energy +6 (9 / 100)
```

The unknown energy, then. Whatever it is, the interface wants it.

He finds it everywhere once he knows to look.

His mother, Su Qinghe, carries water from the courtyard well every morning, and on cold days she presses two fingers to the wooden bucket and the skim of ice on its surface shivers and slides aside on its own. His aunt, a brisk woman with dirt under her nails and a widow's plain white hairpin, walks the herb terraces at dawn with a fan of yellow paper slips, and where she tears one, mist gathers out of clear air and falls as fine rain over the beds. His father sits up late at night at a low desk, drawing curling red characters on yellow paper with that brush, his left hand trembling so badly he has to brace it with his right. Many of the slips crumble as he finishes them. Some do not. Those he stacks carefully in a lacquered box.

The household lamps in the main hall are not lamps at all but small paper charms pasted inside glass, giving off a steady white light that never flickers and never needs oil. The kitchen fire is lit each dawn with one of those yellow slips. When the courtyard fills with fallen pine needles, a handful of older children stand in a ring, make a twisting gesture with their hands, and a small, breathless whirlwind gathers the needles into a heap while a gray-bearded man with a bad hip barks at them to keep their wrists loose.

Below the house, on a packed-earth yard by the gate, a broad young man in leather armor drills thirty village men every second morning. The men are ordinary farmers, but they carry straight swords whose edges shimmer faintly when they strike, and when the young man shouts an order they slap their palms against bronze arm-guards and a ripple of pale light rises over each of them like a soap bubble. The young man himself is Fourth Uncle, Lin Wenshi, the youngest of the Patriarch's sons. When he swings his own sword, the air in front of it splits with a thin silver arc that cuts a practice post cleanly in half from three paces away.

Lin Jian, eight months old and propped in a basket at the edge of the yard, watches this with an expression the village women find very funny.

"Look at the little one," they say. "He wants to be a swordsman."

He does not want to be a swordsman. He wants to know how a thin arc of nothing cuts wood from three paces away. He wants to know what is in that sword, and that brush, and that paper, and why a cup of water has none of it.

He learns the word for it before his first birthday, listening to the gray-bearded man lecture the children in the courtyard.

"Qi," the old man says, tapping his chest. "The breath of heaven and earth. It is in the air, the water, the soil, the stones under this hill. A mortal lives his whole life surrounded by it and never feels it. A cultivator draws it in, refines it, and stores it here." He taps below his navel. "With it, he can do what you have seen. Light a fire. Call rain. Cut with a sword he has not swung. And live a long time. That is what we are. That is what the Lin Clan is."

That night, the panel updates.

```
[Environmental Analysis Updated]
Unknown Energy reclassified: Spiritual Energy (Local Term: Qi)
Properties: Ambient, absorbable by living organisms with compatible channels, storable in specific materials
Compatibility with Fabrication Module: Under Analysis
```

\ \ \*

By his second year he can walk, badly, and talk, carefully. He makes himself speak the way a child speaks: short words, simple sentences, and more mistakes than he needs. A one-year-old who speaks in full sentences would be a wonder. Wonders are watched.

He meets the rest of his family in pieces.

His elder brother, Lin Feng, is six years older: a lean, serious boy with their mother's sharp eyes, who already sits in meditation every morning with the gray-bearded teacher. Lin Feng looks into the cradle the first time with deep suspicion and announces that his new brother looks like a radish. The name sticks. Lin Feng uses it with a gruff, proprietary affection, the way he might name a dog.

His aunt with the rain slips is Third Aunt, Lin Wenqing, who manages the herb gardens and the clan's small stock of medicines, and who has a son, Lin Bo, a cheerful boy of ten who always saves the last rice ball at dinner for whichever child is youngest at the table.

And there is Second Uncle.

Lin Wenhai is round and soft-handed, with a neat beard and a ready smile, and he keeps the account books. He is always pleasant to the baby, always bringing small sweets and patting his head. But by now Lin Jian has begun to feel something he does not have words for in either language: a faint, constant pressure around every person, like warmth off a stove. His grandfather's is vast and steady and old. His father's is weak and frayed. His mother's is cool and quiet, like deep water.

Second Uncle's never matches his smile.

On summer evenings, Grandfather sometimes carries him up onto the eastern wall to watch the sun go down over the valley. The old man does not talk much, but he talks to the baby, perhaps because the baby cannot repeat anything.

"Look there," he says one evening, pointing with his pipe. Below them the hill falls away in green steps: the rice terraces, the herb beds, the long roofs of the village where two thousand mortal families live under the Lin Clan's protection. Beyond the river, the land rises again into forest, and beyond the forest, blue and enormous against the sky, the Beast Mountains. "A hundred and fifty years ago, all of this belonged to iron-backed wolves. My grandfather came up that road with a sword and nothing else. He was a rogue cultivator with three elements in his root and no master. He killed the wolf king on the spot where the main hall stands now, and he built the first wall with his own hands." He taps the stone beneath them. "This wall. He used to say the hill was not a gift. It was a responsibility. Hold the hill. That was all he ever asked of us."

He is quiet for a while. The pipe smoke drifts east.

"He reached Foundation Establishment in under ten years," the old man says, more softly. "No one has done it since. Not his son. Not me." He looks down at the small face in his arms. "Perhaps you, little builder. Who knows?"

Lin Jian looks out at the darkening mountains and feels, for the first time, that this place is not simply somewhere he has landed. It is a structure, old and cracked and load-bearing, and it is holding up everyone he can see.

At two years and four months, Lin Jian is allowed to sit in the corner of the main hall during the family council, because he is too young to understand anything.

Five people sit at the table: Grandfather, Father, Second Uncle, Third Aunt and Fourth Uncle. Second Uncle reads from his account book in a pleasant, rounded voice.

"The Azure Cloud Sect's autumn tribute is three hundred low-grade spirit stones," he says. "The treasury holds one hundred and ninety. The shop's income fell again this season. The Zhao family on Red Ridge has cut its talisman prices for the third time. Their steward has repeated his offer to lease the eastern herb terraces."

"No," says Grandfather.

"Father, with respect, we will be a hundred and ten short—"

"We will find it. The terraces are not for lease."

Third Aunt's mouth tightens. Fourth Uncle stares at the table. Father, beside his own father, says nothing at all, and his left hand trembles slightly on his knee.

Lin Jian, playing with a wooden horse in the corner, watches Grandfather's face and learns that the Patriarch is a hundred and nine years old, that the elders of their realm rarely live past a hundred and twenty, and that the old man plans to make one last attempt at something called Foundation Establishment before his time runs out.

He also learns that spirit stones are money, and power, and the thing the whole family is short of.

After the council, when the adults have gone, he finds the tribute chest by the wall. It is not locked. Inside, in neat rows, lie small gray-white stones like river pebbles, each glowing faintly from within.

He has been waiting a long time for this.

He presses his palm to the nearest stone, focuses, and lets the blue line sweep.

```
[Scan: Low-Grade Spirit Stone]
Composition: Crystalline silicate matrix, saturated with Spiritual Energy
Energy Density: High
Analysis: Compatible power source for Fabrication Module
Warning: Host energy channels unopened. Transfer impossible.
Creation Energy +4 (21 / 100)
```

A power source. The interface can run on these. Not yet, not while his body has no way to channel the energy, but someday.

He is about to take his hand away when the panel keeps going.

```
[Secondary Analysis: Crystal Growth Pattern]
Defect density: elevated
Layering indicates source deposit weakening over time
Projected decline of source vein: 2.6% per year
Viable output remaining: approximately 23 years (±4)
```

Lin Jian sits very still beside the open chest, his small hand on the glowing stone.

The stone came from the vein beneath this hill. The vein that feeds the rice and the herbs, that lets his family cultivate, that is the reason this hill is worth anything at all.

It is dying. In twenty-three years, give or take, it will be gone.

Across the hall, his grandfather has come back for his pipe. The old man stops in the doorway and looks at the toddler sitting by the tribute chest, staring at a spirit stone with an expression no child of two should wear.

"Little builder," he says softly. "What are you looking at?"

Lin Jian looks up at him. In the old man's tired, proud face he sees the whole weight of the family, and he decides that he is the only one who knows, and that for now it will stay that way.

"Pretty rock," he says.

His grandfather laughs and carries him off to bed. The panel glows faintly behind his eyes all the way down the dark corridor.

Twenty-three years, Lin Jian thinks. Then I have twenty-three years.
